searchText: <@!301186049323958275> If you make an AA-typed transaction and target an AA contract, the contract decides validity and chooses the gas limit/price. This uses the EOA's nonce. If you send a normal untyped transaction to an AA contract, you'd use the EOA's nonce, and the EOA would pay for gas. <@!689161464829050960> Hmm, I thought external calls into AA contracts isn't allowed in phase 0? It is possible I'm getting phases mixed up. > If you send a normal untyped transaction to an AA contract, you'd use the EOA's nonce, and the EOA would pay for gas. Would this just be like any other contract call? So the contract would need to have an entrypoint that accepted a signature I guess, but that isn't so bad. You are correct, not in phase 0, but _if_ we allow external calls (possible with `RESERVE_GAS` and/or access lists) you can get the behaviour you want, I think. > So the contract would need to have an entrypoint that accepted a signature I guess, but that isn't so bad. And that entrypoint would need to have its own replay protection. I'm not sure I follow. If `msg.sender == shr(-1, 12)`, it's an AA transaction and the contract needs to check the signature in the calldata, and that signature _should_ sign over the nonce. If `msg.sender != shr(-1, 12)`, it's a normal transaction, and the contract doesn't need to do any signature checking. What is `msg.sender` in the context of a root AA call? `0xffff...` And why do you `shr(-1, 12)`? Oh, I see. That's what's in the EIP, and I can never remember exactly how many f's that is ^^;; Just a confusing way to see if `msg.sender` is `0xfff...`. > If `msg.sender != shr(-1, 12)`, it's a normal transaction, and the contract doesn't need to do any signature checking. If the goal is sponsored transactions this doesn't work. The owner of the AA account needs to provide a signature authorizing the call, and that signature needs to be not replayable. In your terminology, is a sponsored transaction one that is paid for by the contract itself, but `msg.sender` or `tx.origin` is set to an EOA? Sponsored Transaction: Action is authorized by user A, but gas is paid for by user B. Right, but specifically is `msg.sender` or `tx.origin` set to A or B? User A. B *only* pays for gas. They otherwise don't show up in the transaction at all and have no control over anything and should be assumed to be malicious. Yep. I knew that as meta-transaction, and yeah, it isn't supported by our EIP. Ah, we have been trying to rename "meta transactions" to "sponsored transactions" to be more clear about what they are/do. "Sponsored transactions" is a much better name. So my concern is that sponsored transactions is a pretty desirable feature, and we want it to be *compatible* with AA I think. It is pretty easy (IMO) to get sponsored transactions at layer 1 without AA, but it is unclear to me how we could make sponsored transactions work with AA. Yeah... You could do it as an ERC (if I understand the terminology) with AA pretty easily. Hmm, how would you make it work via a standardized contract interface with AA? You'd need some agreed upon proxy contract (or a precompile) at some known address. The AA sponsor contract would get the transaction, do whatever checks it wants before `paygas` to decide if it's willing to pay, then call the proxy contract passing the inner calldata and signature. The proxy contract would check the signature and calldata, then call the real target of the inner transaction, passing the sponsee's address and the calldata. Finally the real target would check that `msg.sender` is equal to the proxy's address. Wouldn't work for existing contracts, obviously. We explicitly didn't want to touch sponsored transactions with EIP-2938, but we'd be happy to explore that road if AA sans-sponsored-transactions isn't desirable enough. What is `ORIGIN` for AA contracts in all call frames other than the first? Bleh, I found the answer and I'm very sad. Surprised <@!273808422753796097> was OK with this given their previous comments on the matter. > If `ORIGIN (0x32)` is invoked in any frame of execution of an AA transaction it must return `AA_ENTRY_POINT`. This means that contracts can discriminate on AA transactions vs EOA transactions, which historically has been quite problematic for contract wallet adoption. I would much rather see `ORIGIN` equal the AA account address. However, to maintain `ORIGIN` semantics, we would need `AA_ENTRY_POINT` to also equal `tx.target`. What is the argument against having `ORIGIN` and first call frame `CALLER` being `tx.target`? We would still be able to do the prefix check with `if (CALLER == this)` I believe. I think we wanted AA and EOA to be distinguishable? Basically because existing apps that are EOA-only do that to prevent transferability whereas anything in an AA is transferable because the AA itself could be transferable That just results in people doing: ``` // don't allow any contracts to participate require(tx.origin != 0xfff...); ``` but yeah, in the long run things that demand untransferability will require a different approach.... right but the point is that being AA-friendly means you can't have any non-transferability I don't have a problem with breaking all of those things... 😬 heh 😛 That pattern totally against the ethos of "your keys, your assets". I feel like if we allow people to differentiate between AA and EOA we are going to end up with significant problems with adoption because a lot of apps are going to openly disallow AA accounts. For example, USDC will likely disallow AA because it breaks their ability to censor. Same with all of the apps that have really terrible security practices where they think that EOA only means that the callers cannot game the system by running some code first. And if we have a whole segment of contracts disallowing AA, then I worry we'll see the same adoption problems we see today with contract wallets. right, that's fair I'm all for supporting more features in the first hardfork containing AA. I think we (Quilt) were afraid of proposing something too large and scaring off the coredevs. Yeah, I totally get that. The problem is that the current proposal may not implement enough to get core devs excited enough about it to want to implement it. We have the EIPs up for `IS_STATIC` (enables `STATICCALL` into AA contracts) and `SET_INDESTRUCTIBLE` (enables `DELEGATECALL` out of AA contracts.) Is a sponsored transactions EIP on top of EIP-2938 where we want to go next? For AA to win my vote (over Rich Transactions) I would like to see/understand a clear path to: 1. Inability for contracts to discriminate on AA vs EOA (this sounds like it is political rather than technical) 2. Support for stealth sponsored transactions (someone else pays for gas, but ORIGIN/CALLER is AA account). 3. Ability to do external static calls before `PAYGAS` (sounds like this is already partially solved, I need to look into the solution still) 4. Maybe more I can't think of at the moment. 😬 > 1. Inability for contracts to discriminate on AA vs EOA (this sounds like it is political rather than technical) I think making EOA-only contract *by default* accept AAs could solve ~75% of this; at least prevent the current problem where there's already-existing applications that won't accept AAs > 3. Ability to do external static calls before PAYGAS (sounds like this is already partially solved, I need to look into the solution still) this is definitely a tougher one. The thing that's partially solved is the ability for external contracts to call _into_ an AA contract. What you're asking for seems to be an AA contract being able to call an _external_ contract before PAYGAS, which is tougher (what is your usecase for that btw? Is it just libraries, or something else too?) > I think making EOA-only contract *by default* accept AAs could solve ~75% of this; at least prevent the current problem where there's already-existing applications that won't accept AAs <@!273808422753796097> What do you mean by this? You mean making it so new accounts are all AA unless you go way out of your way to make not-EOA? Oh I mean the ORIGIN = target change for example (which I think you proposed above) That would make _existing_ EOA checks accept AAs But you would still be able to check for EOA-ness by checking `extcodesize(caller) == 0` Eh, I think as long as it is possible to discriminate people *will* discriminate. > But you would still be able to check for EOA-ness by checking `extcodesize(caller) == 0` Bleh. One fun thing we could do is force-convert all the EOAs into AA contracts which have a "change my own key" function Can we do that live? So users would have to jump through hoops to prove their account's nontransferability sure why not One poke at a time, like the state clearing in 2016 We would need legacy transactions to still work with the AA accounts I think. Else pre-signed transactions from a while back would cease to work. What is the legitimate (non-discriminatory) use case for extcodesize? > What is the legitimate (non-discriminatory) use case for extcodesize? Solidity uses it to check to verify that what you're calling actually is a contract, I think? I like the idea of converting everyone's account to AA automatically and removing the ability to have non-AA accounts. Then I would be fine with ORIGIN being `0xffff...` as there would be nothing to discriminate on. In full AA, is there a legitimate use case for legacy EOA support? Is it possible to make it so transactions signed and saved a year ago will continue to work with an account that was migrated to AA? Perhaps something that will convert legacy transactions to an AA transaction under the assumption that they are using the default AA contract (that we auto-migrated everyone to). Is it possible to *change* the contract code for an AA account? Or is the code at it permanent? Hmm, everyone being migrated to AA *would* break some contracts. There are some standards out there for tokens that support both EOA and contract, and the behavior is different. I believe this is fine, but only if we allow users to *change* their AA contract code. That way, a user could add support for certain callbacks later (like checking to see if a particular contract supports X). How much trouble would we cause if, for AA transactions, the ext code family of opcodes, pointed at the AA contract, return what they would for an EOA? then we would need to have an explicit AA contract type which we currently do not <@!273808422753796097> Why would we need to know if the contract is AA? Return zero from `EXTCODESIZE` if `addr == tx.target`.

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content:
<@!301186049323958275> 

If you make an AA-typed transaction and target an AA contract, the contract decides validity and chooses the gas limit/price. This uses the EOA's nonce.

If you send a normal untyped transaction to an AA contract, you'd use the EOA's nonce, and the EOA would pay for gas.

You'd need some agreed upon proxy contract (or a precompile) at some known address.

The AA sponsor contract would get the transaction, do whatever checks it wants before `paygas` to decide if it's willing to pay, then call the proxy contract passing the inner calldata and signature.

Finally the real target would check that `msg.sender` is equal to the proxy's address.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
For AA to win my vote (over Rich Transactions) I would like to see/understand a clear path to:
1. Inability for contracts to discriminate on AA vs EOA (this sounds like it is political rather than technical)
2. Support for stealth sponsored transactions (someone else pays for gas, but ORIGIN/CALLER is AA account).
3. Ability to do external static calls before `PAYGAS` (sounds like this is already partially solved, I need to look into the solution still)
4. Maybe more I can't think of at the moment.  😬
